Moluccan snapper Lutjanus boutton reaches a maximum fork length of 35 cm [Li = 35 cm] in females, a size that defines the upper boundary of somatic growth for this tropical lutjanid. Field studies in the Banda Sea indicate that this asymptotic dimension is typically attained after several years of sustained feeding on crustaceans and small teleosts. The corresponding ultimate wet body weight calculated from this length is 570 grams [Wwi = 570 grams], a mass that is modest relative to some larger congeners such as Lutjanus argentimaculatus but characteristic of medium-bodied reef predators. This size-weight relationship was derived from a length-weight regression specific to the species, and it places adult females in a range where they can efficiently exploit crevice-dwelling prey. Observations of marked individuals suggest that growth rates slow considerably once this fork length is approached, with most somatic energy thereafter directed toward reproductive functions rather than continued increase in structural size.

At the onset of sexual maturation, female Moluccan snapper first become reproductively active when they reach a fork length of 16 cm [Lp = 16 cm], a relatively modest size compared to the ultimate length. This fork length at puberty corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 55.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 55.7 grams], indicating that individuals begin allocating resources to gamete production well before completing somatic growth. Histological examinations of gonadal tissue from specimens collected across the species range confirm that vitellogenesis commences at this body size, and the transition is marked by the initial appearance of cortical alveoli in oocytes. This early onset of maturity is an adaptive strategy common among short-lived tropical snappers, allowing individuals to contribute to the next generation even if they do not survive to reach the maximum recorded size. The relatively low mass threshold for puberty suggests that first reproduction can occur within the first few years of life for most females.

The maximum reproductive output of Lutjanus boutton has been estimated from comparative fecundity data obtained for the congener Lutjanus carponotatus, with adjustments made for differences in body mass. At a stable water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], females release approximately 60,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 60,000 eggs per spawning event] and spawn approximately 8 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 8 times per year] during peak spawning periods, yielding an annual fecundity that can exceed half a million eggs per reproductive season. Such high fecundity is typical of marine teleosts that produce pelagic eggs, where larval mortality is substantial and only a tiny fraction of offspring survive to recruitment. The sustained production of eggs at this rate places considerable energetic demands on mature females, especially during the warmer months when metabolic rates are elevated under the same thermal regime.

Newly fertilized eggs of this species are pelagic and transparent, hatching into yolk-sac larvae that rely entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth for a freshly hatched larva is 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a mass that is consistent with the small egg diameter typical of lutjanids and derived from measurements made on the related species Lutjanus stellatus. This minute initial weight reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo, which are completely absorbed within a few days post-hatching. At this stage, the larva is approximately 2 to 3 millimeters in total length and must begin feeding on small planktonic prey such as copepod nauplii soon after mouth opening to avoid starvation. The low birth weight also imposes a high vulnerability to predation during the early larval phase, as the small body size offers limited escape capability from planktivorous invertebrates and larval fishes.

Maximum lifespan in Lutjanus boutton has been determined through analysis of annual increments in sagittal otoliths, with the oldest recorded individual reaching an age of 10 years [am = 10 years] in the wild under the thermal conditions typical of its distribution (28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]). This longevity is intermediate among Indo-Pacific snappers, falling below the 30-year lifespans observed in some large-bodied lutjanids but exceeding the short-lived pattern of smaller reef-associated species. The age-at-death data indicate that natural mortality is relatively high during the first year of life, but survivors experience a gradual senescence that limits maximum lifespan to this decadal boundary. Annual growth rings become increasingly narrow as fish approach this age, reflecting the deceleration of somatic growth that accompanies the plateau in fork length at 35 cm. With roughly eight to nine reproductive years available, the species relies on high annual fecundity to buffer against the elevated juvenile mortality typical of pelagic egg producers.
